title: Keep an Eye on the Fringe
author: Admired Leadership
summary: The argument here is that innovation is a peripheral phenomenon before it is a mainstream one, and that this holds as much for businesses and non-profits as it does for music, fashion, art and technology. The practical consequence is a scanning discipline: attending to nascent technologies, unconventional practices and fast-rising competitors, and asking specifically what others are doing that looks unorthodox or offbeat. The piece is direct about the risk it is guarding against, that conventional practice blinds an organisation to what is possible, and that by the time a trend has gone mainstream the window for an effective response has usually closed. It assigns the work to the whole team rather than to the leader alone, framing horizon-scanning as a shared obligation. A useful qualification follows: this is not an argument for taking every new idea seriously, but for extracting insight from the fringe without being obliged to adopt or react to it. Gibson's line about the future being unevenly distributed supplies the closing frame.
points: The structural claim is that innovation reliably appears on the periphery first, which makes the mainstream a lagging indicator and a poor place to look for what is coming.
The timing argument is the sharp one: once a trend is mainstream it is usually too late to respond effectively, so the scanning has to happen while the signal still looks marginal.
Responsibility is distributed to the whole team rather than reserved to the leader, making horizon-scanning an ongoing shared task rather than a strategy offsite.
The qualification matters as much as the claim: the point is to harvest insight from the fringe, not to adopt or react to every unorthodox practice encountered.
The named risk is self-inflicted, that conventional practice itself is what blinds an organisation to what the next new thing might be.
quotes: Innovation begins on the fringe, not in the mainstream. Emerging trends appear on the periphery of whatever is popular and well-accepted.
The best leaders hunt for the future by learning what is happening outside the normal ropes.
They recognize that conventional practices blind them to what is possible and what the next new thing might be.
By the time a new trend becomes mainstream, it is often too late to respond effectively.
Leaders and teams that fall asleep at the wheel of their success can pay the ultimate price.
Knowing what is occurring on the boundaries of established practices is essential work for leaders and teams.
